record.paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: Causal fairness often treats social categories such as race or gender as variables that can be intervened on. When, if ever, do such social categories admit meaningful interventions, and how should fairness methods handle cases where counterfactual manipulation of those categories is morally, politically, or causally ill-defined?

evidence.quote: From a social science perspective, it is heavily debated whether social categories admit interventions.

Hu [197] argues that causal theories about social categories such as race involve “ineliminable substantive moral and political considerations, a feature for which interventionism can not well account”.

More broadly, Kasirzadeh and Smart [199] review various papers at this intersection between sociology and causal modeling, concluding that social categories often do not admit counterfactual manipulation.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Counterfactual fairness frameworks model a protected attribute A (such as race or gender), other covariates X, and an outcome Y within a structural causal model M = (U, V, F), where V = {A, X, Y}, U denotes exogenous variables, and F is a set of structural equations. A predictor f(X, A) is said to be counterfactually fair if, for every individual with observed values (A = a, X = x) and every alternative value a' of the protected attribute, the distribution of the counterfactual predictor f(X_{A <- a'}, a') given (A = a, X = x) coincides with the distribution of f(X, A) given (A = a, X = x), where X_{A <- a'} denotes the value of X under the intervention do(A = a'). This definition presupposes that interventions do(A = a') on the protected attribute are well defined.

Formulate criteria under which a social category encoded by such a protected attribute A admits a well-defined intervention do(A = a') in a structural causal model, and identify the situations in which no such intervention is meaningful (for example, because A is constitutive of other variables in V, because counterfactual manipulation of A is not uniquely specified, or because the manipulation is morally or politically ill-posed). For the latter case, propose and justify a notion of fairness, expressible in the language of (possibly modified) structural causal models, that does not rely on counterfactual manipulation of A but still captures discrimination involving A, and prove or characterize its consistency with standard observational and interventional fairness criteria when interventions on A are in fact well defined.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a conceptual/foundational open problem at the intersection of causal inference, fairness in machine learning, and social science. Recent work (e.g., Kasirzadeh & Smart 2021; Hu & Kohler-Hausmann; Kohler-Hausmann 2019) argues social categories such as race often do not admit well-defined counterfactual manipulation, and proposals like "fairness through awareness" or constitutive (rather than causal) accounts have been advanced, but no consensus formal framework exists. The problem is widely regarded as open.

status_evidence.title: The Use and Misuse of Counterfactuals in Ethical Machine Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Kasirzadeh and Smart argue that social categories like race often do not admit counterfactual manipulation in the manner required by counterfactual fairness.
status_evidence.claim: Recent scholarship concludes the question of intervening on social categories remains contested and unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Eddie Murphy and the Dangers of Counterfactual Causal Thinking About Detecting Racial Discrimination (Kohler-Hausmann)
status_evidence.snippet: Argues that race is a constitutive social category and that counterfactual interventions on race are not well defined.
status_evidence.claim: A leading argument that interventions on race are ill-posed, supporting that the problem is open.

status_evidence.title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys highlight the manipulability of social categories as an unresolved open problem in causal fairness.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is explicitly listed as open in the causal ML literature.
